name: Argan oil

lead: Argan oil is pressed from the kernels of the argan tree (Argania spinosa), native to Morocco and southwestern Algeria. It is rich in oleic and linoleic acids and contains vitamin E, and has been sold in cosmetics since the early 2000s.

People use it on hair for shine and smoothness and on skin as a light moisturiser. A few forum users apply it to eyebrows hoping for growth; reviews have not found significant evidence for hair growth.

paras: It is applied directly or found in shampoos, conditioners, creams and lip products. People massage a small amount into hair lengths or skin. Trials have also had postmenopausal women take it by mouth or apply it to skin.
Allergic reactions are uncommon, but a letter reports protein contact dermatitis from argan oil. Adulteration with cheaper oils prompted Moroccan purity testing for exports in 2012.

angle.text: As an emollient it adds shine and softness to hair and moisture to skin. Brow-growth claims on forums are not backed by published studies.

lead: Argan oil is a plant oil pressed from the kernels of the argan tree (Argania spinosa), which grows in Morocco and southwestern Algeria. Moroccans eat it with bread, couscous and pasta, and since the early 2000s it has become a common cosmetic ingredient in face creams, lip glosses, shampoos, moisturisers and soaps [1]. It is among the best-known natural oils for hair and skin care.

For appearance, people use it as an emollient. Applied to hair lengths it adds shine, softness and a smoother, less frizzy look; applied to skin it acts as a light moisturiser that leaves the surface feeling soft [1][2]. Cosmetic argan oil is made from unroasted kernels, while culinary oil comes from roasted kernels [3]. Chemically it is about 99 percent triglycerides, with oleic acid (42.8 percent) and linoleic acid (36.8 percent) as the main fatty acids, plus tocopherols (vitamin E), phenols, carotenes and squalene [1].

Research includes small randomised trials in postmenopausal women on skin elasticity and moisture [4][2], reviews of plant oils for skin barrier repair [5][4], and a 2022 systematic review of hair oils that found no significant evidence for argan oil on hair growth, hair quality or infestation, while noting that dermatologists often let patients keep using hair oils because side effects are unlikely [6]. On forums such as looksmax.org, it is mentioned as a cheap brow and hair oil [7]. Production by Moroccan women's cooperatives, UNESCO recognition of the argan know-how in 2014, and adulteration concerns are part of its wider story [1][8].
infobox: 30 to 50% of the kernel; about 40 kg of dried fruit per litre [1]
Over-the-counter cosmetic ingredient and food oil

paras: The argan tree is the only species in its genus and is native to the semi-arid south-west of Morocco, with some populations in southwestern Algeria [1]. Argan oil is non-refined virgin oil; kernels give 30 to 50 percent oil, and roughly 40 kg of dried fruit are needed for a litre [1][3].

A review of its quality control describes two products: cosmetic oil from unroasted kernels and food oil from kernels roasted for a few minutes and then cold pressed [3]. Beyond triglycerides it contains small amounts of tocopherols, phenols, carotenes and squalene [1]. A 2024 review of cosmetic oils reports tocopherol content of 60 to 90 mg per 100 g and that about 19 g per 100 g of its fatty acids are saturated [9]. A skin-barrier review notes that oils with a higher linoleic-to-oleic ratio are considered to have better barrier-repair potential, while oleic-rich oils may be less favourable, which is the context in which argan's roughly balanced oleic and linoleic content is discussed [4].

Cosmetic products containing argan oil include face creams, lip glosses, shampoos, conditioners, moisturisers and soaps [1]. Reviews place argan alongside olive, coconut and jojoba oils as plant oils valued for hydrating, shielding the skin surface and limiting moisture loss [9], and alongside other oils studied for anti-inflammatory and barrier effects [5][4].

People apply argan oil as a light moisturiser. Its look-and-feel benefit is a softer, more supple skin surface from the lipid film it leaves and from its vitamin E content [9]. Traditional Amazigh use includes moisturising skin against desert conditions [8].

Argan oil is a staple of hair-care routines for shine, smoothness and frizz control, either as a pure oil or as a component of leave-in serums and conditioners [1]. A T Nation poster in a 2011 thread observed that a hair product containing argan oil and silicones would likely make hair shiny and tame frizz [10]. A looksmax.org thread asks about argan and coconut oil for keeping grown-out hair from puffing out [11]. A T Nation hair-loss protocol thread lists argan oil with deep conditioning as an add-on to improve hair appearance, separate from its follicle-focused steps [12].
Some forum users apply argan oil to eyebrows hoping for thicker, longer brows (see Claims and evidence) [7].

Argan oil has long been part of the diet, personal care and traditional medicine of Amazigh (Berber) communities in the Arganeraie region of south-west Morocco. UNESCO inscribed 'Argan, practices and know-how concerning the argan tree' on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014; the listing describes rural 'argan women' passing on extraction skills to their daughters, with steps of harvesting, drying, pulping, grinding, milling and mixing with warm water [8]. The oil is also given as a wedding gift and used in festive dishes [8].

Cosmetic demand grew rapidly after the first US sales in 2003 [1]. Production is estimated to support about 2.2 million people in the region, much of it through women's cooperatives, with around 300 small firms, mostly cooperatives, operating as of 2020 [1]. Forecast output was 17,802 tonnes in 2022, up from 4,387 tonnes in 2014 [1]. Mechanical extraction can produce oil at lower cost than cooperatives [1].

Argan trees provide food, shade and shelter, and are said to help prevent desertification and soil erosion [1][3]. Wikipedia reports that women workers, mostly Berber, often earn little, that chemistry professor Zoubida Charrouf has advocated higher pay, and that L'Oreal has pledged to source from fair-trade cooperatives [1].

Supplies were found to be diluted with cheaper oils such as sunflower oil, and from 2012 the Moroccan government began random purity testing of export shipments [1]. A review of argan oil's quality control discusses chemical composition and extraction as factors in assessing authenticity and grade [3].

Allergic reactions to topical argan oil appear uncommon. A 2023 letter in the journal Dermatitis described protein contact dermatitis caused by argan oil [13]. The 2022 hair-oil review notes that dermatologists often accept hair oils because adverse effects are unlikely [6].

Skin: a randomised trial in postmenopausal women examined dietary and/or cosmetic argan oil and skin elasticity [2], and a clinical study in a similar population examined its moisturising effect on skin [14]. A further randomised trial in postmenopausal Moroccan women looked at the vitamin E profile [15].

Hair: a systematic review of 22 articles on coconut, castor and argan hair oils concluded that argan oil does not have significant evidence supporting hair growth, hair quality improvement or treatment of infestation, while coconut oil had clinical support for brittle hair and infestation [6].

Other trials of dietary argan oil have studied antioxidant and lipid status in hemodialysis patients [16] and knee osteoarthritis symptoms [17]; these concern health outcomes rather than appearance. A 2024 review also describes possible effects on gut and skin microbiota while noting that mechanisms are not fully understood [18].
